findings.summary: The cover's bottom icon-strip is clipped by the page edge, slicing the second line of every caption in half.
findings.evidence: First caption reads "Images &" with its continuation ("Registry") sheared mid-glyph at the bottom edge; the descriptive lines under the other five icons ("build an index…", "shell holding…", "the DNS…") are cut to a sliver of their ascenders.
findings.fix: Reduce the cover's vertical stack (title/subtitle/logo/callout block) or increase the bottom padding of the render so the full two-line icon strip fits inside the 1080×1440 frame.

findings.summary: Cross-references cite syllabus chapter numbers instead of the deck's actual page numbers, so every "page N" pointer sends the learner to the wrong slide.
findings.evidence: Page 5 callout: "Networking namespaces get their own page (9)." — but page 9 is "Container Cleanup and Dockerfile Basics". Page 8: "Exit **137** = 128 + 9: killed by SIGKILL, often ==OOM== (page 3)" — OOM/cgroups is on page 4, page 3 is "Build-Ship-Run Flow and Namespaces". Page 10: "deps before source: cache hits (page 7)" — page 7 is "Multi-arch Images and Container Lifecycle"; page 9: "(fix on page 13)" and page 10: "(page 12)" point to pages that do not exist in this part.
findings.fix: Renumber every inline reference to the real slide number within this part (OOM → page 4, SIGTERM fix → page 10), and for topics not in this part (networking, build cache, security) replace "page N" with a named forward pointer such as "covered in the Networking notes later in the series".

findings.summary: The "What Docker Is" chapter's summary appears at the end of page 2, before its example (typical flow) and mistakes sections on page 3.
findings.evidence: Page 2 closes with the checkbox block "Docker = ==standardized== shipping format for apps" / "Image → container → registry; CLI → dockerd → containerd → runc", while page 3 then delivers "4. Typical Flow" and "5. Common Mistakes" for the same chapter.
findings.fix: Move the checkbox summary block to page 3, after the "5. Common Mistakes" bullets and the OCI callout, so the chapter reads definition → mechanism → comparison → example → mistakes → summary.

findings.summary: The namespace table presents user-namespace uid remapping as standard container behaviour, but Docker does not enable the user namespace by default.
findings.evidence: Namespaces table row: ["`user`","uid 0 mapped to ==unprivileged== host uid","real root"]
findings.fix: Mark the `user` row as opt-in: "only with `--userns-remap` or rootless mode; by default container uid 0 **is** host uid 0" — which is also why page 5's "container isolation is not VM security" point matters.

findings.summary: `ptrace` is listed as blocked by the default seccomp profile, but Docker has allowed it by default since 19.03 on kernels 4.8+.
findings.fix: Replace `ptrace` with a genuinely blocked example such as `kexec_load`, `init_module` or `bpf`; Docker docs note ptrace is only blocked on kernels older than 4.8 (moby commit 1124543, Docker 19.03).

findings.summary: The container-internals chapter's summary is placed on page 4, before its example and mistakes sections on page 5, so the chapter is wrapped up before it is finished.
findings.evidence: Page 4 ends with the checkbox summary "container = ==namespaces== (isolation) + ==cgroups== (limits) + ==overlay== layers (filesystem)", yet page 5 then opens "5. Example: the PID 1 problem" followed by "6. Mistakes" — and the unheaded PID 1 bullets ("Kernel gives PID 1 no default signal handlers") sit on page 4 above that summary, splitting the PID 1 topic across the summary.
findings.fix: Move the checkbox summary block to the end of page 5, after "6. Mistakes" and the container-vs-VM table, and keep the unheaded PID 1 bullets adjacent to "5. Example: the PID 1 problem" by giving them a numbered heading ("5. The PID 1 problem") and placing them immediately before the tini example.

findings.summary: The Dockerfile chapter's opening definition is stranded at the end of page 8, ahead of the container-lifecycle chapter's mistakes and summary on page 9.
findings.evidence: Page 8's final block reads "A ==Dockerfile== is a plain-text recipe of instructions; `docker build` executes them **top to bottom**, committing a layer per step, to produce an image." — then page 9 opens with "5. Common mistakes" about `docker run`/`attach`/`logs` and "6. Cleanup and takeaways" before returning to "1. Key Concepts" for Dockerfiles.
findings.fix: Move the Dockerfile definition paragraph from the end of page 8 to page 9, directly above the "1. Key Concepts" cards, and let page 8 end with the "Sticky tip" callout.

findings.summary: VM boot time is stated as minutes, which overstates typical VM startup and contradicts the deck's own later figure.
findings.evidence: Container vs VM table: ["Boot","minutes","milliseconds"] — while page 5 says VM "start time" is "seconds to minutes"
findings.fix: Change the page 2 cell to "seconds to minutes" so it matches the page 5 table (microVMs boot in well under a second).

findings.summary: NET_BIND_SERVICE is described as granting only port 80, when it permits binding any privileged port below 1024.
findings.fix: Reword to "keeps only the ability to bind privileged ports (<1024)".

findings.summary: The cgroups shell example is not runnable: inline comments follow the line-continuation backslashes, so the backslash escapes a space instead of the newline and the command breaks after the first line.
findings.evidence: Code lines: "docker run -d --name web \\", "  --memory=512m \\  # RAM cap", "  --cpus=1.5 \\     # 1.5 cores"
findings.fix: Move the annotations out of the continued command (e.g. put `# RAM cap`, `# 1.5 cores` in the block's `note`, or on their own comment lines above), leaving `\` as the last character on each continued line.

findings.summary: The bullet states containers on Windows are always Linux processes in a VM, ignoring native Windows containers.
findings.evidence: "Expecting native containers on Mac/Windows: **Docker Desktop** runs a Linux VM; containers are Linux processes inside it"
findings.fix: Qualify as "Linux containers on Mac/Windows run inside a Linux VM (Docker Desktop); only Windows containers on Windows use the host kernel natively".

findings.summary: Page 5 relies on Dockerfile instructions and the shell-form/exec-form CMD distinction five pages before the Dockerfile chapter defines them.
findings.evidence: Page 5 code: "RUN apk add tini" / "ENTRYPOINT [\"tini\",\"--\"]" / "CMD [\"node\",\"server.js\"]" and the mistake "Shipping a shell-form CMD as PID 1: signals never reach the app" — `CMD`/`ENTRYPOINT` and shell vs exec form are first explained on page 10 ("shell / exec form | `/bin/sh -c` wraps | direct, gets ==signals==").
findings.fix: On page 5, add a one-line gloss to the code note — e.g. "ENTRYPOINT/CMD are Dockerfile instructions (page 10); the bracket form runs the binary directly" — and rewrite the mistake bullet as "Letting `/bin/sh -c` be PID 1 instead of your app: signals never reach it (forms explained on page 10)".

findings.fix: Either drop the `--build-arg` line from the page 9 build-command example and add it to the page 10 ARG bullet, or annotate it on page 9 as "passes a build-time variable declared with `ARG` (page 10)".

findings.summary: The claim that only `-p` maps host ports ignores `-P`, which publishes exactly the ports `EXPOSE` declares — so EXPOSE is not purely documentation.
findings.evidence: "Believing `EXPOSE` publishes; only `-p` maps host ports" and "`EXPOSE 8000` only **documents** the port"
findings.fix: Amend to "`EXPOSE` does not publish on its own; `-p` maps a chosen host port, and `-P` publishes every `EXPOSE`d port to a random high host port".
